                                      I.      INTRODUCTION
       As shown on the Applicants “Interest Routes” map, 1 the routes that are supported by parties

who have actively participated in this proceeding can be grouped broadly into three “corridors”

based on where they cross the Colorado River:

       •     The “Northern Corridor” routes (Routes 392 and 410) cross the Colorado River while

             paralleling an existing high-voltage transmission line along Segment U3.

       •     The “Central Corridor” routes (Routes 487, 891, and 894) cross the Colorado River

             in close proximity to Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks along either

             Segment J11 (Route 487) or Segment J22 (Routes 891 and 894).

       •     The “Southern Corridor” routes (Routes 296, 572, and “Cherokee Creek G”) cross

             the Colorado River close to an existing pipeline ROW along Segment J31.

                                                    1
        Staten Realty, LLC (“Staten Creek Ranch,” Party #390) strongly supports Routes 392 and

410, both of which follow a “Northern Corridor” that would avoid running this line well within a

mile of Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks, cross the Colorado River while paralleling

an existing transmission line, and take a superior path across open, developed land in the north end

of McCulloch County rather than clearing a new 200-foot right-of-way (ROW) through

undeveloped, densely wooded ranchlands like Staten Creek Ranch. A comprehensive evaluation

reveals that the Northern Corridor routes travel through an area that is much more compatible for

transmission infrastructure, and would only marginally increase the cost of this line and its impact

on habitable structures. As detailed below, this is a case where the Commission should place

substantial weight on the qualitative impacts that this proposed transmission line would have on

the unspoiled natural beauty of two of Texas’s premier state parks rather than focusing myopically

on the incrementally better quantitative performance of routes along the Central Corridor. Finally,

while Staten Creek Ranch does not believe that the Southern Corridor routes perform as well as

those in the Northern Corridor, Staten Creek is unopposed to those routes, as they would at least

mitigate the extreme qualitative downsides of the Central Corridor routes while performing

similarly on a quantitative basis.

                            II.      ARGUMENT AND AUTHORITIES
       A.        The Commission should not select any of the Central Corridor routes,
                 including the Applicants’ suggested Route 894 and Staff’s suggested Route
                 487.
                 1.      The Central Corridor routes would all cause significant and

when routing transmission lines. 2 That factor should receive substantial weight in this proceeding

 because certain routes, 3 including all routes that use the Central Corridor, 4 would severely impact

both Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks. Collectively, Colorado Bend and Post Oak

Ridge State Parks cover approximately 8,500 acres on either side of a section of the Colorado

River. 5 Colorado Bend State Park attracts tens of thousands of visitors each year, 6 and Post Oak

Ridge, which is not yet open to the public, is expected to attract tens of thousands more. 7 These

visitation numbers are unsurprising, as the area in and around those parks is known for its natural

beauty, which is currently unmarred by large infrastructure like high-voltage transmission lines. 8

Dr. Andrew Sansom, a former Executive Director of TPWD, referred to Colorado Bend as “one

of the most treasured State Parks in Texas,” 9 and there is ample evidence in the record to support

that claim. 10 Similarly, Post Oak Ridge State Park is also of great importance to the state of Texas.

That park “was one of the first three parks acquired using the voter-approved $1 billion Centennial

Parks Conservation Fund, underscoring the public significance of this resource.” 11 Additionally,

Post Oak Falls, which is located just across the Colorado River from the southwestern corner of

Post Oak Ridge State Park, is a popular scenic and recreational feature that the ALJs in Docket

No. 37448 weighted similarly to Enchanted Rock and Colorado Bend State Parks and sought to

                          d.       Commission precedent strongly supports avoiding impacts to
                                   state parks and the scenic natural areas surrounding them.
        Texas state parks are an invaluable public resource, and much of that value comes from

providing the public with an opportunity to escape highly developed landscapes and experience

unspoiled natural beauty. In prior CCN cases, the Commission has repeatedly emphasized the

value of avoiding or minimizing impacts to state parks. And importantly, the Commission has not

ignored the fact that placing a line in the immediate vicinity of a park still impacts the public’s use

and enjoyment of that area.

                                   i.    In Docket No. 38290, the Commission prioritized
                                           qualitative impacts to Palo Duro Canyon over
                                           quantitative routing factors.
        In Docket No. 38290, Commission selected a route for a 345 kV CREZ line that was much

longer, much more expensive, and more impactful to habitable structures in order to avoid Palo

Duro Canyon. Importantly, in that case, “the proposed routes [did] not encroach directly on the

Palo Duro Canyon State Park,” 48 but some of the routes (including the utility’s proposed route)

would have crossed the canyon “within roughly three to four miles of the park entrance,” 49 and

“these lines would [have] likely be[en] visible from portions of the park.” 50 As such, it was

apparent that the Commission placed great weight on the visual impact of a transmission line on
